final_text:
The one that matters most is **#5 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

Why it stands out for this project:

- **It is the clearest worked example of your project's core idea.** The whole paper is about a forecast *triggering* action: pre-El Niño forecasts flagged a high-risk marine heatwave, an expert workshop judged it severe, and that triggered a pre-emptive rescue of 25 red handfish in January 2024. That forecast → assessment → response chain is exactly the "early warning" logic your project is building toward.
- **It shows the value of lead time, with hard numbers.** During the event, in-situ temperatures exceeded records — 80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C) — and the fish were held for 3 months and released after the heatwave subsided, with post-release survival confirmed after 2 months. It's a concrete case of why warning lead time translates into real outcomes.
- **It's recent and current** (2026, still open), and it's Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species — a citable precedent for proactive, forecast-driven management that you can point to when making the case for your early-warning system.

The other strong candidates, for context:

- **#3** (comment on the Northeast Pacific seasonal ocean forecasting system, 2026) is the most methodologically relevant — a ~10 km MOM6-based seasonal forecast system with 32-year retrospective evaluation, ACC > 0.5 for lead times of several months, and routine real-time forecasts starting October 2026. If your question is "what does a good early-warning *system* look like," this is the one to read.
- **#6** (1–14-day ML MHW forecasts in the Northern Bay of Bengal, 2026) is the closest to your ML-for-data-assimilation interest, but it's a B.S. thesis dataset on Zenodo with a thin abstract, so it's more of a data resource than a key reference.

My take: **#5 for the "why it matters" argument, #3 for the "how to build it" argument.** If you want, I can pull the full text of either and dig into the methods.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

final_text:
Here's my comparison:

**#1 – A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS)**
- €50M, deadline 2027-02-16
- Focus: strengthening the *infrastructure* of global ocean observation — deploying equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, technology roadmaps with industry, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions (polar, deep sea, areas beyond national jurisdiction).
- The emphasis is on the *observing system itself*: making it resilient, open, and strategically autonomous for Europe.

**#2 – Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean**
- €5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23
- Focus: *scientific understanding and projections* of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean region — ocean–atmosphere–sea-ice–ice interactions, decadal-to-millennial climate projections, tipping points, ecosystem vulnerability, and improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models.
- The emphasis is on *research questions and modelling* specific to one region.

**Which fits the Marine heatwave early warning project better?**

Neither is a perfect match, but **#1 (GOOS)** is the closer fit. Here's why:

- Your project is about *early warning* — which depends on having reliable, continuous observations and operational forecasting systems. #1's core ask (strengthening observing networks, OSEs/OSSEs, data delivery, operational services) maps directly onto what an early-warning system needs.
- #2 is regionally locked to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean, and its scope is dominated by long-term projections, ice dynamics, and tipping points. That's a different timescale and a different region than what a marine heatwave early-warning project typically targets.

That said, #1 is a €50M call — likely a large consortium — and its primary framing is geopolitical/strategic (EU autonomy, GOOS governance). If your project's core contribution is the *machine-learning forecasting and data-assimilation* side rather than the observing infrastructure, the fit is partial. You'd want to position your work as the "data delivery and forecasting service" component of a broader observing-system proposal.

**Bottom line:** #1 fits better, but neither grant is a natural home for a project whose centre of gravity is ML-based marine heatwave forecasting. If you're weighing these, #1 is the one to build a proposal around; #2 would only make sense if you had a strong Antarctic/Southern Ocean angle.

The clear standout is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most for Plastic pathways:

- **It's the only item on the slate directly about marine litter.** The rest of the feed is phytoplankton, ocean forecast systems, turtle telemetry, and remote sensing — none of which touch debris pathways.
- **It's a working tool, not just a paper.** The deposit contains a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated results behind every number in the manuscript. That's a ready-made component for modeling how plastic reaches shore.
- **It's validated against field records** from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories — so the kernel has been tested against real beaching observations, not just synthetic cases.
- **It's reproducible.** The deposit includes a reproduction manifest with a checker, and the full particle trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are available on request if you want to dig into the setup.

The practical angle: if your project involves particle-tracking plastic transport and beaching, this kernel is a drop-in candidate for your OceanParcels pipeline, and the code is open.

One caveat: I can't see the project's confirmed state or open blockers in this conversation, so I'm judging fit from the project's purpose alone. If you'd like, I can pull up the full project review — goals, blockers, milestones — and tie the slate items to each open blocker.

Here's what I found.

## Best fit: #4 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open grants in your slate, #4 is the closest to the Plastic pathways project (#2). The call asks for systemic solutions to reduce pollution and environmental degradation in ports, under the Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" — marine litter tracking and debris pathways are a natural entry point. It's still open, with a deadline of **21 September 2027**, and €1M–€8.9M available.

The other open grants are further afield:
- **#10** (waterborne transport / zero-carbon fuels) — about fuel spills and decarbonization, not debris pathways
- **#7** (coastal resilience to climate change) — about flooding, erosion, sea-level rise; pollution is a secondary outcome
- **#5** (biotech recycling of plastics) — about recycling technologies and enzymes, not environmental tracking

**Biggest doubt:** #4 requires demonstration in at least 4 ports across four different sea basins, with strong involvement of port authorities and public bodies. That's a heavy consortium requirement for a project whose core is satellite-based debris tracking. You'd need to frame the pathways work as the scientific backbone of a broader port-pollution action.

## Who should lead

No one in the lab has a declared profile that directly covers #4's requirement slots. The nightly ranking puts:

1. **Jonah Whitcombe** (#15) — closest match (64%). He declares marine litter and Lagrangian analysis, which are the core of the Plastic pathways project. He's the natural lead for the scientific content.
2. **Priya Raman** (#16) — close second (63%). She declares satellite oceanography and coastal water quality, which supports the remote-sensing and monitoring side.

I'd suggest **Jonah leads the application** with Priya co-leading the remote-sensing/monitoring workstream. You, as PI, would anchor the consortium and the port-authority partnerships.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** the port-authority and public-administration roles the call explicitly asks for. Those need to come from outside.

## Who outside the lab

I can't suggest specific people outside the lab right now — collaborator search is turned off on this instance. What I can say is what the call needs you to find:

- **Port managing authorities** from at least 4 ports, one in each of the four basins (Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, Danube/Black Sea)
- **Public administrations** with meaningful involvement (the call strongly encourages this)
- **Industry partners** (the call asks for scientific and industry partners together)

You could look at the Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" lighthouse ports listed in the call text, or at existing EU port-circularity projects, to identify authorities already active in this space. If you turn on collaborator search in the app, I can match specific people to those roles.

# Judging a call's fit

   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.

   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, what's new for it, and one funding opportunity worth a look.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project's members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but its confirmed state (goals, method, stage, milestones, open blockers) is empty in Mycelium right now. That means either it hasn't been filled in yet or it hasn't been confirmed recently, so I can't tell you how far along it is. If you'd like, you can add or update that in the app, and I'll be able to give you a proper status review next time.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the project's slate this week:

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-point item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If your project tracks where floating debris ends up, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on or compare against.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, *Remote Sensing*). Relevant on the methods side: a YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that detects and segments low-contrast, curved features in MODIS imagery at high accuracy. The same detection-and-segmentation pattern applies to spotting debris plumes or filaments in satellite imagery.

3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (2026). Relevant as the ocean-model side of the pairing: a daily operational forecast system analysis. If Plastic pathways couples a circulation model with particle tracking, this is a useful reference for how such systems are run and evaluated in practice.

(Also on the slate: #7, a comment on an EGU paper, and #9, a multi-agent tracking paper — both less clearly tied to debris pathways, so I've left them out of the top three.)

## One funding opportunity

**#8 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC), NSF** — still open, deadline **15 February 2027**.

- **Why it fits:** OTIC funds unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. A tide-resolving beaching kernel or a satellite-based debris detection pipeline is exactly the kind of reusable observational/analytical capability it looks for, and it matches the lab's declared debris-pathways cluster (#13).
- **The biggest doubt:** OTIC leans toward *technology development* rather than a single study. The proposal would need to frame the work as a tool or method the wider ocean-science community can adopt, not just a project deliverable.
- **What I couldn't check:** the full eligibility rules (institution type, citizenship, sub-award limits) and the budget ceiling — those aren't in what I can see, so it's worth reading the program description (PD-98-1680) before committing.

A longer-term alternative on the slate is #12 (Horizon, integrating remote sensing and in-situ observations, €3–8M, deadline 22 September 2027), but its focus is biodiversity data integration, so the fit is looser than OTIC's.

If you'd like, I can dig into any of these papers in full, or walk through who in the lab might lead the OTIC proposal.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

**For #11 (Sandia fellowship):**

This is a direct ML-for-ocean-forecasting evaluation paper, exactly the kind of data-driven, benchmarked work the fellowship calls for. It would demonstrate hands-on experience with ML forecasting methods and rigorous evaluation against baselines.
- Alternatively, **#34 — "Data-Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing"** (Reiss et al., 2026, GRL) would be a strong complement if the applicant wants to show ML applied to a physical parameterization problem with spatial block cross-validation — a more "computational science" flavor.

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

#30 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The global ocean observing system faces risks to continuity, openness, and resilience due to evolving geopolitical dynamics, reduced engagement by key international partners, and structural gaps in under-observed regions like the deep sea and polar regions, which threatens scientific sovereignty an…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) through the deployment of observation equipment, performing observing system experiments (OSEs) and observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs), applying network optimization approaches, co-creating technology roadmaps with industry, and in…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observing frameworks, specifically the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

#34 [paper] Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
Authors: Rafael Sebastian Reiss, Lisanne Blok, Nicholas Leonard, Kate Oglethorpe, Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, Colm-cille P. Caulfield, Ali Mashayek
Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl123721
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic Ocean turbulent mixing is poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding, despite its importance for regional dynamics and global overturning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training gradient-boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data to predict turbulent dissipation from hydrographic variables, using spatial block cross-validation for evaluation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles) for training; pan-Arctic hydrographic observations and high-resolution model output for application.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

Authors: Minjong Cheon, Kaoru Kakinuma

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational cost of Earth system models limits the exploration of scenarios and ensemble members, while existing machine-learning weather models coupled to oceans have produced weak El Niño variability or relied on climate-model output, and none effectively routes climate impacts through…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model using a coupler named YAHO that links a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon, and energy components constrained by observations; the model uses an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave oc…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Simulations of approximately 1,000 years on one graphics processing unit; evaluation against observed climate data from 1979-2022; routing of runoff to 212 river gauges; and future projections for SSP1 and SSP3 scenarios for the period 2081-2100.
Abstract:
Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#38 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

#41 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

final_text:
The clearest fit in the Plastic pathways feed is **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most:

- **It is the only item on the slate squarely about marine litter transport.** The rest touch the project at best tangentially — #12 (loggerhead turtle movement) and #11 (lake hydroclimatic trends) are about other tracers or other systems, and #3, #9 (phytoplankton/NPP) are about biology, not debris.
- **It gives you a concrete, reusable method.** The deposit contains a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript (#4, abstract). That is directly usable for modelling how plastic reaches shore.
- **It is validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching observations at Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories (#4, "Setting") — exactly the kind of ground-truthed approach a pathways project needs to trust its predictions.
- **It is reproducible.** The deposit includes a reproduction manifest with a checker, and the large trajectory and flow-field files are available on request (#4, abstract).

One caveat: the project's confirmed state (goals, blockers, milestones) is not visible to me in this conversation, so I can't tie #4 to a specific open blocker. If the team's current bottleneck is, say, predicting where debris accumulates on shore, #4 is the item to read first.

Suggested next steps for the team:
- Read #4 and its companion manuscript, and check whether the OceanParcels kernels can be dropped into your existing particle-tracking setup.
- If the project's state in the app is more than thirty days old, refresh it so the slate keeps ranking against current goals and blockers.

final_text:
Both are open, and both are Horizon Europe calls with 2027 deadlines, so timing isn't the deciding factor. The difference is what each one is actually asking for.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
This call is about the *infrastructure* of ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, and technology roadmaps with industry, all coordinated under GOOS. It explicitly wants to close structural gaps in under-observed regions — polar regions, the deep sea, areas beyond national jurisdiction — and to strengthen Copernicus Marine Service. The emphasis is on *building and sustaining the observing system itself*, with biodiversity and climate resilience as the outcomes it serves.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
This call is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Antarctic and Southern Ocean: ocean–atmosphere–sea ice–ice dynamics, decadal-to-millennial projections, tipping points, and ecosystem vulnerability. It explicitly asks for work on *extreme events* and mid-latitude weather, improved monitoring indicators, and long-term continuous monitoring systems for the region.

**Which fits Marine heatwave early warning (#3) better?**

#2 fits better, for one concrete reason: it asks for *projections and understanding of extreme events* in a defined ocean region, which is exactly what a marine heatwave early-warning project does — forecast what the water will do next and hand that to decision-makers. The call's language on "extreme events," "near-, mid- and long-term" changes, and "monitoring indicators that support decision-making" maps directly onto the project's problem and method.

#1 is a weaker fit because it is primarily an *infrastructure and deployment* call. It wants new observation equipment, OSEs/OSSEs, and network optimization — the project's focus is on *forecasting and data assimilation*, not on building the observing network. The project could contribute to #1 (e.g., as a user of the observing system, or via OSSEs to test forecast skill), but that would be a secondary role, not the core of the proposal.

**The biggest doubt on #2:** it is regionally bounded to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. If the project's heatwave work is focused on other regions (e.g., the Bay of Bengal, as in #8, or coastal waters more broadly), the geographic scope is a real constraint. You'd need to frame the proposal around Southern Ocean heatwaves specifically, or show how the project's methods transfer there.

**What I could not check:** the full eligibility rules for either call (consortium size, country eligibility, SME participation requirements) and the project's current milestones or budget, which would matter for a realistic proposal plan.

results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#28 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Floating debris transport in marginal seas is controlled by a combination of geostrophic currents, wind-driven currents, wave-induced drift, and direct wind forcing, but the relative importance of these processes remains difficult to quantify without in-situ trajectory observations. This study evaluates near-surface forcing combinations for particle tracking in the East/Japan Sea using 33 GPS-tracked surface drifters deployed off the Korean coast in November 2021. The drifters revealed a clear cross-basin transport pathway toward the Japanese coastline and an early bifurcation near a hyperbolic-type Lagrangian structure. We used a particle tracking model to test combinations of geostrophic current, Ekman current, Stokes drift, and windage against the observed drifter trajectories using MAE and NCLS metrics. For undrogued DX drifters, the best performance was obtained by combining geostrophic current, Stokes drift, and windage. For drogued DO drifters, which sampled a deeper effective depth, the inclusion of all four forcing components provided the best agreement with observations. The optimized forcing combinations outperformed benchmark simulations driven by the GOFS analysis and GLORYS reanalysis in this specific event, primarily because they better reproduced the Lagrangian structure associated with the early trajectory bifurcation. Seasonal simulations showed that winter winds enhance eastward transport and beaching along Japan, whereas weaker summer winds allow mesoscale eddies to broaden particle dispersion. The present framework represents the fluid-dynamical component of near-surface particle transport and does not explicitly include plastic-specific fate processes such as fragmentation, biofouling-induced buoyancy changes, aggregation, settling, or resuspension.

Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new and one funding angle.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project is a lab project with three members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. However, Mycelium has no confirmed state recorded for it: no goals, method, stage, milestones, or blockers are on file, and I can't see when that was last reviewed. If the team has been working on it, that context may be out of date — it can be filled in or corrected in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers

From the project's current slate (all entered this week):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-topic item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea using ROMS flow fields. The deposit includes the code, experiment scripts, and aggregated results — a ready-made reference for particle-tracking methodology and a potential collaboration or validation target.
2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Not about plastic, but a strong methodological parallel: a YOLO11-based detector (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that achieves an 86.00% F1 for detection and 87.55% for segmentation on low-contrast, curved ocean features in MODIS imagery, applied over a decade of data (2011–2020). Useful if the project wants to detect or track debris plumes or surface features from satellite imagery at scale.
3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array"** (2026). Relevant as the in-situ observing-system side of the story: basin-scale trends from a large autonomous sensor network. It speaks to how Plastic pathways could ground its particle-tracking and remote-sensing work in independent in-situ validation at scale.

The other new slate items (#4, #5, #7, #9) are further afield — Arctic phytoplankton, a regional forecast system, a comment piece, and a multi-agent tracking paper — and I'd rank them lower for this project.

## One funding opportunity

**#12 — "Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework"** (Horizon, CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01). Still open, deadline **22 September 2027**, €3–8M.

- **What fits:** the call asks for multisensory data-integration systems that harmonise in-situ observations with satellite remote sensing, with a focus on predictive analytics and AI, including marine ecosystems under pressure. A plastic-pathways project that couples particle tracking with satellite detection and in-situ validation maps naturally onto that "from sensor to AI to policy" framing, and pollutants/sea use are explicitly named as pressures to address.
- **The biggest doubt:** the call is biodiversity-centric — its expected outcomes are about ecosystem condition, habitat mapping, and biodiversity trends. The proposal would need to frame plastic pathways as a driver of ecosystem degradation (e.g., impacts on marine habitats and species) rather than purely as a transport-and-fate study, to sit comfortably inside the biodiversity typology it requires.

One thing I couldn't check: the call's eligibility rules (EU member/associated country requirements, consortium composition) aren't visible to me here, so that's worth confirming before committing to a draft.

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#12 [grant] Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Now I have a clear picture. Let me put this together.

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #19 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System

**Why it fits Plastic pathways (#18):**

The project's core concepts — marine litter tracking, satellite ocean remote sensing, Lagrangian particle tracking, and beaching — map directly onto what #19 asks for: strengthening and operationalising the global ocean observing system, with emphasis on data delivery, network optimisation, and closing structural gaps in under-observed regions. The grant is €50 M, deadline **16 Feb 2027**, and explicitly calls for proposals that bring together observation communities, marine research infrastructures, and technology providers.

The other open grant on the slate, #26 (NSF OTIC), is narrower — it funds instrumentation development for the ocean science community. It could be a secondary target if the project develops a specific sensor or tool, but #19 is the stronger strategic fit for a project that combines satellite observation, Lagrangian modelling, and beaching analytics.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

| Person | Role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **You (Mara Ellison)** | **PI / lead** | Declared: data assimilation with ML, ocean extremes. Mycelium's ranking names you as covering "stabilise, further strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" via your data-assimilation + ML work. As PI you also carry the strategic framing. |
| **Priya Raman (#4)** | **Co-lead / satellite & remote-sensing work package** | Declared: satellite oceanography, coastal water quality. Mycelium's ranking names her for the same observing-system slot via satellite ocean-colour remote sensing. She is the natural owner of the satellite-observation work package. |
| **Jonah Whitcombe (#3)** | **Modelling / Lagrangian work package** | Declared: marine litter, Lagrangian analysis. He covers the particle-tracking and beaching-modelling side of the project. |

**Gaps the nightly ranking flags (no one in the lab covers):**
- Observing system experiments (OSEs) / OSSEs
- Network optimisation approaches
- Areas beyond national jurisdiction
- Industry partner (a role the call asks for but no profile matches)

You'll want to recruit or partner to fill those.

---

## Potential external partners

Based on the papers Mycelium has in the corpus that overlap with the project's concepts:

1. **Erik van Sebille** (co-author of #37, *Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic*, Ocean Science 2026) — works on Lagrangian transport of floating macroplastic and coastal interaction dynamics. A natural fit for the modelling/transport work package and for the "areas beyond national jurisdiction" gap.

2. **Philippe Cecchi / Pierrick Penven** (co-authors of #34, *Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire*, Marine Pollution Bulletin 2026) — use a coupled CROCO + Ichthyop Lagrangian framework for plastic dispersal and beaching. Strong methodological overlap with the project's Lagrangian particle-tracking concept.

3. **Sara Rivero-Calle / Daniel Koestner** (co-authors of #33, *Plastic polymer classification with shortwave infrared reflectance*, Marine Pollution Bulletin 2026) — develop hyperspectral SWIR and machine-learning approaches for polymer-type identification of marine debris. This could fill the "floating debris detection" gap that no lab member currently declares, and add a technology/remote-sensing angle the call values.

4. **Eimear Magee / Douglas Marques** (co-authors of #36, *Advances in technologies across the marine plastic value chain in Europe*, Cleaner Engineering and Technology 2026) — a broad review spanning satellite/drone remote sensing, robotic platforms, AI-driven classification, and recycling. Useful for the industry/technology-provider partner role and for framing the circular-economy angle the call expects.

5. **Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls / Leandro Bugoni** (authors of #30, *Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island*, Thalassas 2026) — work on marine-litter baselines and monitoring protocols in a remote, beyond-national-jurisdiction setting. Could help address the "areas beyond national jurisdiction" gap.

---

**Suggested next steps:**
- Confirm with Jonah and Priya that they want to be named on the proposal.
- Reach out to Erik van Sebille and Philippe Cecchi first — their methods overlap most directly with the project's Lagrangian/beaching core.
- Identify an industry or technology-provider partner (the call explicitly asks for one) — the authors of #36 or #33 may know suitable SMEs or instrument companies.
- The deadline is **16 Feb 2027**, so you have roughly three months.
