#29 [paper] UAV-based deep learning and spatial analysis for mapping coastal plastic debris distribution
Authors: Elnur Safarov, Эмиль Р. Байрамов, S.H. Safarov, Etibar Gahramanov, Saida Aliyeva, Zaur Imrani
Venue: Geocarto International
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2026.2736384
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Plastic waste accumulation in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins with restricted hydrodynamic exchange.
Method (Mycelium's reading): UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea.
Abstract:
Plastic waste accumulation is a major environmental challenge in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins where restricted hydrodynamic exchange can promote long-term litter retention. This study assesses surface macroplastic litter along the Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea using UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis. A total of 7,192 litter items were detected within approximately 0.385 km2, corresponding to an average density of 18,684 items/km2, while hotspot densities exceeded 60,000 items/km2. The distribution was strongly clustered, with a Nearest Neighbour Index of 0.49 and three shore-parallel accumulation zones. Detected litter was spatially associated with shoreline proximity, low-relief terrain, and reed-dominated vegetation, particularly desiccated reed belts exposed by recent Caspian Sea-level decline. Because the survey represents a single-date observation, these relationships are interpreted as spatial associations rather than direct causal mechanisms. The workflow supports targeted cleanup and monitoring across semi-enclosed coastal environments and broader evidence-based environmental management.

#30 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring
Authors: Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls, Leandro Bugoni
Venue: Thalassas An International Journal of Marine Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41208-026-01266-2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#33 [paper] Plastic polymer classification with shortwave infrared reflectance: Opportunities and limitations for remote sensing of marine debris.
Authors: Ohall, Ashley, Koestner, Daniel, Bisson, Kelsey, Brandes, Jay, Garaba, Shungudzemwoyo P, Rivero-Calle, Sara
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42600411/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic debris or litter poses urgent environmental, socio-economic, and human health challenges, yet tools for polymer-specific detection with optical remote sensing remain limited. To advance optical classification capabilities, the newly curated and comprehensive MArine Debris spectral reference Library (MADLib) collection was used to evaluate three existing algorithms and develop two proof-of-concept approaches for polymer type classification with hyperspectral shortwave infrared (SWIR) reflectance measurements. A stepwise classification framework was designed to identify seven polymer types from hyperspectral reflectance data, known as the six-step polymer identification (SSPI) algorithm. SSPI achieved an overall classification accuracy of 89%, which declined to 73 ± 1% when simulated Gaussian noise was added to the measurements. Although performance declined under simulated noisy conditions, the framework establishes a foundation for future refinement through other avenues, such as spectral matching or machine learning methods. A multispectral polymer type classifier (MSPC) approach was also developed and evaluated using machine learning methods to leverage diagnostic features in SWIR reflectance data from only eight moderately-broad bands. A shallow neural network showcased strong performance for a subset of the seven most represented polymers in MADLib under the relatively restrictive testing procedures explored, achieving consistent and noise-robust class accuracies over 80%. The MSPC approach highlights the promise of compact multispectral systems for efficient and scalable polymer type identification. Overall, this work highlights both the potential and current limitations of reflectance-based polymer type identification and guides the next generation of remote sensing approaches for marine plastic debris.

#37 [paper] Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic
Authors: Marc Schneiter, Rolf Hut, Erik van Sebille
Venue: Ocean science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3595-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the transport and coastal interaction dynamics of floating macroplastic in intertidal regions, specifically through the analysis of drifter groundings.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Field campaign involving the release and tracking of 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea; manual and statistical automatic detection of drifter groundings; characterization of groundings relative to wind conditions, tides, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind.
Abstract:
Abstract. We study floating marine macro plastic pollution with a dedicated campaign where we released and tracked 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region where water dynamics are driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind. The campaign captured water surface transport patterns, and around 150 observations of the drifters interacting with the coast and mudflats, where groundings of varying durations occurred. We identify these transitions in the recorded trajectories from both manual inspection and by formulating and evaluating a statistical approach for automatic detection. We then characterize the transitions by relating them to the coinciding wind conditions and tides, and with the duration of the groundings. The results of this analysis generally agree with the intuitions that wind towards the coast increases the frequency of interactions and that the drifters are rarely re-floated during falling tides. Furthermore, we find that groundings tend to be shorter duration when they occur shorter before the next high tide. We present multiple visualizations that characterize the groundings in more detail. The results provide a statistical characterization of coastal interactions that can be integrated in models and used for the planning of beach-cleanups. They may be improved by considering the specific environmental conditions of the campaign, and by analyzing the influence of the weight and size of the drifters, which are both larger than typical floating macroplastic.

#34 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

## Best-fitting open grant

Two open grants are on the project's slate, and one is clearly the better fit:

**#15 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50M, deadline **2027-02-16**).

Why it fits #7 Marine heatwave early warning:
- The project's core is **ocean data assimilation** and **marine heatwave prediction** — both are things the call explicitly asks for: "stabilise, further strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" and reliable, fit-for-purpose data delivery.
- Your declared strengths map directly onto its expected outcomes: data assimilation + ML for ocean forecasting (you) and satellite ocean remote sensing (Priya) both feed "strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities and data coordination."
- It's a large, multi-partner, EU-led call — which is exactly the shape that lets you bring in the pieces your lab doesn't cover (below).

The other open grant, **#10 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)** (deadline 2027-02-15), is a poorer fit: it funds **instrumentation development with broad applicability** to ocean science. The project is a forecasting/assimilation effort, not an instrumentation one, and Mycelium found **no lab member whose declared profile covers its core slot**. I'd treat #10 as a secondary option only if you have a concrete instrument to build.

## Who in the lab should lead

**You (Mara Ellison)** should lead the #15 application.
- Your declared **ocean data assimilation** is the single strongest match to the call's central requirement, and the nightly ranking named you as a top profile fit.
- You're the PI and a member of the project, so you own the narrative.

**Priya Raman** should be a co-lead / second author: her **satellite ocean remote sensing** is the other declared strength the call rewards, and she's the natural lead on the observing/remote-sensing work package.

**Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (physics-informed ML) and **Sun-hee Park** (ocean data tools) round out the team — Tomás on the ML-assimilation method, Sun-hee on the data infrastructure/dashboards. Note the project's declared concepts include **sea surface temperature** and **fisheries**, which no member currently declares — worth confirming who actually owns those before you submit.

## Who outside the lab to partner with

The call has two gaps no one in your lab covers — **observing system (simulation) experiments (OSSEs)** and **network optimisation** — plus an explicit **industry** role. Based on the papers in your slate, the strongest external partners are:

- **The OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team** (Gregory C. Smith, Fabrice Hernández, Charly Régnier, et al. — #28). They run a decade-long intercomparison of operational ocean forecasts against common observational datasets — directly the "operationalise the observing system" and verification angle the call wants. A natural anchor partner.
- **NASA's aquatic/marine data-assimilation community** (Susanne E. Craig, Frank Muller-Karger, Leonid Shumilo, Tzortziou Maria — #29). Their decadal strategy pairs "Numerical Models and Data Assimilation" with "Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data" — a strong fit for both the assimilation and the data-infrastructure work packages.
- **The Ocean-E2E group** (Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang — #33), who do end-to-end neural assimilation for global marine-heatwave forecasting — a direct methodological complement to your ML-assimilation approach.
- **The Korean coastal early-warning group** (Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong — #22; and Huitae Joo, Byeong-Jun Lim, Hae Kun Jung — #32), who have demonstrated operationally actionable marine-heatwave early warning for aquaculture — useful for the "reliable services / impact" outcome.

#22 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

Abstract:
Abstract Near real-time evaluations of operational predictions are required to ensure consistency and quality of forecasts. When possible, intercomparisons of such predictions against common observational datasets allows a further understanding of multi-system spread and uncertainty in predictions, and sheds light on quality of both numerical prediction and observational datasets. For the physical ocean, an intercomparison of operational analyses and forecasts was put in place in 2012 under the auspices of the OceanPredict Intercomparison and Validation Task Team. With over a decade of experience demonstrating the evolution of the accuracy of operational oceanographic predictions, this valuable dataset provides a community resource to underpin additional studies such as the benchmarking of deep-learning neural-network emulators. Here we highlight the lessons learned and challenges encountered in this activity and describe how the system is evolving from a research effort into an operational verification activity. We also describe two additional datasets that have been added, namely, sea ice concentration and 15-m currents.

Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

#32 [paper] Separating Sensor-like Anomalies from Regional Oceanographic Events: A Machine-Learning-Assisted, Physics-Guided, Event-Preserving Quality-Control Framework for Coastal Buoy Temperature Records
Authors: Huitae Joo, Byeong-Jun Lim, Hae Kun Jung
Venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse14161462
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Coastal upwelling and typhoon-driven mixing can cool a buoy record by several degrees within hours. Sensor faults do the same. Quality-control schemes that flag anomalies by residual magnitude alone therefore risk discarding real events. We analysed 30 min temperature records from six buoys and three depths off the east coast of Korea, spanning 2008–2024, and built a machine-learning-assisted, physics-guided, event-preserving quality-control framework that adds new labels without altering any observation or existing flag. Cooling events were catalogued from changes in the observed surface temperature and in the surface-to-bottom temperature difference and classified using three physically interpretable axes: spatial coherence with neighbouring buoys, vertical consistency between layers, and atmospheric forcing from ERA5 and typhoon best-track data. A station-wise ridge prediction model, fitted to the surface layer at five of the six stations, supplied prediction residuals that served only to flag candidates. Residual magnitude separated sensor-like anomalies from regional-event candidates poorly (direction-free AUC 0.52–0.56); upwelling-candidate and typhoon-related events produced residuals as large as those of the sensor-like reference group, or larger. The physical axes showed much stronger internal operational separability, reaching pairwise AUC values up to 1.000 and a multivariate cross-validated mean AUC of 0.987. These values do not represent external validation because the groups were partly defined using the same axes. The framework preserved regional-event candidates while affecting derived monthly means by at most about 0.0005 °C, yet retained event-scale cooling of up to about 8 °C. Prediction residuals are therefore useful for broad anomaly-candidate detection but insufficient for final event classification, which should rely on physically interpretable, multi-station criteria.

Abstract:
The integration of ocean observing networks and artificial intelligence is changing how and who access marine information. This review looks at technological and recent innovations along with uses from the Argo and Biogeochemical-Argo programs, satellite remote sensing, autonomous underwater vehicles, and cloud-native data architectures. This review assesses the integration of these systems with Artificial Intelligence, particularly large language models enhanced with vector-database retrieval systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This paper discusses the major hindrances to efficient ocean data utilization like data fragmentation, also throwing light on the intricate formats like NetCDF, scalability, and policy barriers. It highlights modern practices such as practical lakehouse architectures, cloud processing, and AI systems with semantic retrieval controls. Furthermore, the review describes and discusses AI prototypes and systems built from case studies designed to assist in disaster response and mitigation, monitor climate, and manage fisheries by transforming data on spectra, profiles, and images into concise answers and easy-to-understand visual response graphics. It also talks about the persisting questions of trust, explainability, provenance, multilingual support, and inclusive engagement at the community level as the foundation of new research. These systems anticipate the provision of standard metadata, uncertainty framing, AI systems, and ethically aligned deployment pathways. Integrating resilient observing systems with human centred AI and scalable infrastructure is essential to realize a transparent, operational, and community-driven ocean-observing ecosystem promoting further research in this domain.

final_text:
The paper that matters most for the Marine heatwave early warning project is **#4 — "Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish"** (Stuart-Smith et al., 2026, Conservation Science and Practice).

**Why it stands out:**

- **It's a real-world proof of concept for your project's core idea.** The paper documents Australia's first pre-emptive rescue of a protected marine species, triggered *by a marine heatwave forecast* ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño. An expert workshop assessed the forecasted extremes (>20°C or +~3°C) as a severe threat, and that assessment triggered the emergency intervention. That's exactly the "early warning → action" chain your project is building.

- **It shows the full loop working:** forecast → risk assessment → decision → intervention → verified outcome. 25 red handfish were captured in January 2024, held for 3 months while in-situ temperatures exceeded records (80 days more than 2°C above the long-term mean), and 18 were successfully returned after the heatwave subsided, with post-release survival confirmed.

- **It's a conservation case study, not a methods paper.** That makes it useful for framing *why* early warning matters — the stakes are species survival — and for understanding how forecast products get translated into decisions by non-forecasters (managers, conservation agencies).

**The runner-up is #5** (Mojumder, 2026), which evaluates 1–14-day ML forecasts of marine heatwaves against persistence benchmarks in the Northern Bay of Bengal. It's more directly about the forecasting method itself, but it's a B.S. thesis data/code release with a thin abstract, so it's less immediately actionable than #4.

If you want, I can pull the full text of #4 to dig into how the forecast was communicated and what the decision process looked like in detail.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

The clear standout for **Plastic pathways** is **#4** — the code and results behind "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo).

Why it matters most:

- **It's the only item on the slate that is squarely about marine litter.** The rest touch the project at best obliquely — #12 (loggerhead turtle movement) and #5 (a regional ocean forecast system) are about tracers in the ocean, and #7 (internal solitary waves) is about wave detection. #4 is about plastic itself.
- **It's a method you can actually use, not just read.** The deposit contains a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, the experiment scripts, and the aggregated result files behind every number in the manuscript. If your project tracks where debris ends up, a beaching kernel is exactly the piece that decides what happens when a particle reaches shore — the part most particle-tracking studies hand-wave.
- **It's validated against field records.** The kernel was developed and tested against beaching records from Uido, South Korea, using ROMS flow fields — so it's not just a theoretical construct, and the reproduction manifest means you can check their numbers.
- **It's fresh and open.** It entered your slate this week (2026-11-10) and is still current.

The one caveat: the raw particle trajectories (~32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (~37 GB) are only available on request, so if you want to rerun their experiments rather than just borrow the kernel, that's a step to take.

final_text:
Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)
This call is about strengthening the *infrastructure* of ocean observation: deploying equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, and co-creating technology roadmaps with industry. Its setting is the GOOS framework, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and the Copernicus Marine Service. The emphasis is on physical and biogeochemical observation capacity, biodiversity monitoring, and EU strategic autonomy in data delivery.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean** (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)
This call is about *understanding and projecting* the future of the Antarctic and Southern Ocean: ocean–atmosphere–sea ice–ice dynamics, improving Earth System Models and regional coupled models, distinguishing human-induced from natural change, and ecosystem vulnerability. It explicitly calls for work on extreme events and mid-latitude weather, and for improving monitoring indicators that feed into assessments.

**Which fits #3 better?**

#2 is the closer fit. The project's core work — marine heatwave forecasting, ML-based prediction, and early warning — aligns with #2's explicit interest in extreme events, improving projections, and developing monitoring indicators. The project's method (data-driven forecasting, evaluation against benchmarks) maps naturally onto #2's call for improving models and reducing uncertainty in projected changes.

#1 is a weaker match. It is infrastructure-first: the project would need to frame its contribution as strengthening the observing network itself (new sensors, OSEs, network design) rather than as a forecasting or prediction effort. The project's slate shows active work on ML forecasts and model evaluation (#8, #13), which is closer to #2's "improve projections" language than to #1's "deploy equipment and optimize networks" language.

**Biggest doubt on #2:** the geographic scope is specifically Antarctic and Southern Ocean. If the project's heatwave work is focused on other regions (e.g., the Bay of Bengal, as #8 suggests), the proposal would need to justify why that work contributes to the Southern Ocean's safe operating space — for instance, through shared methods, coupled-model improvements, or global-scale extreme-event understanding.

**Biggest doubt on #1:** the €50M scale and the infrastructure emphasis mean the project would likely need to be one component of a much larger consortium, and the lead would need to be an observing-network or infrastructure group.

**What I could not check:** the project's confirmed state (problem statement, method, milestones) was not visible to me in this conversation, so I compared the grants against the project's name, its members, and the work visible on its slate. If the project has a formal problem statement or milestone plan that I can't see, the fit judgment could shift.

"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the

#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#4 [paper] A LiDAR-based reconstruction reveals increasing Arctic phytoplankton production during low-light winter-shoulder period.
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Peng Chen, Siqi Zhang, Delu Pan
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej4633
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The authors used 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP). A bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions, and low-light estimates were generated as physically const…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic region, specifically marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions, using spaceborne LiDAR data from 2006 to 2023.
Abstract:
Arctic marine productivity is traditionally considered concentrated in the sunlit season, yet low-light winter-shoulder periods remain poorly constrained because passive ocean color observations require sufficient solar illumination. Here, we use 2.39 million spaceborne LiDAR profiles from CALIOP (2006–2023) to reconstruct Arctic net primary production (NPP) and evaluate how active-sensor observations reduce this seasonal blind spot. The bio-optical retrieval model was trained using MODIS-constrained observations under illuminated conditions; accordingly, low-light estimates represent physically constrained extrapolations beyond the primary MODIS-observable training domain rather than direct NPP measurements. Within this framework, LiDAR increases winter half-year observational coverage from ∼20 to 30% to ∼70 to 75% and reveals widespread low-light winter-shoulder production across marginal seas and seasonal ice-edge regions. Pan-Arctic NPP integrated over this period increased at an estimated rate of 0.75 Tg C year −1 during 2007–2023, whereas the corresponding passive-sensor signal was negligible. Accounting for this component raises annual Arctic NPP estimates by ∼13.3% indicating that passive sensor-based assessments may underrepresent the magnitude and seasonal structure of Arctic productivity. Associations with declining sea ice and surface warming suggest this underrepresented production is consistent with ongoing seasonal reorganization of Arctic carbon fixation. Uncertainties from model parameterization, low-light extrapolation, and limited in situ validation are largest in the lowest-light and highest-latitude regimes. These findings do not imply photosynthesis during absolute polar night, but show that active LiDAR observations with explicit light constraints and transparent extrapolation limits can test how unresolved low-light winter-shoulder production may alter Arctic NPP seasonality under continuing sea-ice loss.

#7 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#11 [paper] Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array.
Authors: Thomas James Ryan-Keogh, Sandy Thomalla
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb0994
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Estimating basin-scale changes in marine net primary production (NPP) while overcoming the limitation of remote sensing, which is restricted to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Using data from the biogeochemical-Argo array of autonomous profiling floats to estimate basin-scale NPP change via the carbon-based production algorithm.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The biogeochemical-Argo array, covering the Atlantic, Southern, and Pacific Oceans.
Abstract:
Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Here's what I found.

## Best fit: #8 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open grants I checked, #8 is the closest to Plastic pathways. It's a Mission "Restore our Ocean and Waters" call (€1M–€8.9M, deadline 2027-09-21) that asks for systemic, place-based solutions to reduce pollution and environmental degradation in ports — with strong involvement of port authorities and local communities. The strongest reason: the project's marine-litter pathway work (beaching, transport, coastal accumulation) maps naturally onto the call's pollution-reduction and monitoring objectives in port areas. The biggest doubt: the call is heavily place-based — it expects demonstration in at least 4 ports across four sea basins, with public bodies as partners — which is a different shape from a modelling/forecasting project, and it's not clear how much of the project's core method (Lagrangian pathway analysis) you'd want to bend into that frame.

The other open grants I checked fit less well:
- #5 (ZEWT, waterborne transport) — about zero-carbon fuel spills and pollution from shipping, not plastic pathways.
- #12 (plastic recycling biotech) — about recycling complex plastics industrially, not ocean transport.
- #19 (Global Ocean Observing System) — about observing infrastructure and GOOS governance; the project's slate has it, but it's a stretch for a pathways project.
- #26 (NSF OTIC) — instrumentation development; US-based, different shape.
- #34 (coastal resilience) — climate resilience and nature-based solutions; adjacent but not about plastic.

## Who in the lab should lead

I have to be honest here: **no one's declared profile directly covers the slots #8 asks for** (port-based pollution solutions, port authority partnerships). The nightly ranking's closest profile matches are:

- **Jonah Whitcombe** (#15) — declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis. He's the natural scientific lead: the project's core method is his declared territory, and he's a project member.
- **Priya Raman** (#16) — declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality; second-closest match, and also a project member. Her satellite angle could carry the monitoring/demonstration component the call wants.
- **You** (#14) — closest match after the two above; as PI you'd be the natural applicant of record.

So: Jonah as scientific lead on the pathways content, Priya on the observation/monitoring workstream, and you as PI holding the application. I can't see anyone's papers or conversation-confirmed skills here, so this is based on declared profiles only.

## Who outside the lab

I can't name specific people: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so no outside suggestions are available to me. What I can say is what the call itself requires as partners, which is where to look:

- **Port managing authorities / public bodies** — the call strongly encourages them as consortium partners, and you need at least 4 ports across the Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, and Danube basins.
- **Local/regional authorities and port communities** in those basins.
- **Industry partners** (the call expects scientific and industry partners together).

If you'd like, I can dig into the project's slate papers (e.g. #23, the tide-resolving beaching kernel) to help frame the scientific case, or check the other open grants in more detail.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

Scope:

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. ## Best-fitting open grant

**#10 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01; €50,000,000; deadline 2027-02-16; still open).

Why it fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#7) better than the others on the slate:
- The call's core ask — *stabilise, strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system, with open data delivery that is fit-for-purpose* — is exactly the kind of work your project does: turning observations into reliable, resilient ocean forecasts. Your data-assimilation-with-ML and SST-extremes work maps directly onto "reliable services" and "climate resilience."
- It explicitly names the **Copernicus Marine Service** and **Essential Ocean Variables** as the frameworks it builds on — the same infrastructure an early-warning system plugs into.
- The other open grants are a poorer match: #9 (NSF OTIC) is about *instrumentation development*, not forecasting; #11 is carbon sources/sinks; #12 is Antarctica/Southern Ocean; #13 is biodiversity data integration; #14/#15 are marine geology/drilling. None of those sit on the heatwave-forecasting core.

One honest caveat: #10 is a large, consortium-scale call (€50M) that leans on observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. Your project's forecasting strength is a strong anchor, but you'd want partners to cover those observing-system and ABNJ angles (see below).

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the requirement-slot check both point to a **two-person lead**:

- **You (Mara Ellison, #2)** — PI. Your declared *data assimilation with ML* and *ocean extremes* cover the call's central "operationalise the observing system / climate resilience" slot, and your ML-assimilation-for-forecasting work is the project's core. You're the natural lead.
- **Priya Raman (#4)** — co-lead on the observation side. Her declared *satellite oceanography* covers the "strengthened global ocean observing capacities and data coordination" slot, and the ranking named her first for the profile fit.

The remaining lab members don't add a distinct slot for this call: Tomás (#6, physics-informed ML / circulation) is a useful supporting voice on the ML-assimilation method, and Sun-hee (#5, ocean data tools) could support the data-delivery/FAIR angle. Jonah (#3, marine litter / Lagrangian) is better matched to the Plastic pathways project (#8) than to this one.

**Gaps no one in the lab covers:** observing-system experiments (OSEs), observing-system simulation experiments (OSSEs), network-optimisation approaches, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. The call also wants an **industry** role. These are the slots to fill with external partners.

## Who outside the lab to partner with

Based on the papers in the corpus that sit on the same ground as this call:

- **The GOOS / OceanOPS community** — the *Global Ocean Observing System Status Report 2026* (#22, Belbéoch, Begg, Fournier, Kolodziejczyk, Post, Prakash, Rusciano, Stukonytė) is the natural anchor for the "stabilise and operationalise GOOS" and "areas beyond national jurisdiction" slots. These authors are the people who maintain the global observing-network picture the call is built on.
- **MonGOOS (Mediterranean GOOS Regional Alliance)** — *The Mediterranean observation systems* paper (#21, Vargas-Yáñez, Pasqueron de Fommervault, Clementi, Ferrarin, Liubertseva, Álvarez-Berastegui, Mourre, Ličer). MonGOOS is a GOOS Regional Alliance that explicitly supports the **Copernicus Marine Service** and **EMODnet**, and its consultation drew on 74 institutions, 4 companies, and the European JRC. This is a ready-made consortium network covering the observing-network and ABNJ angles, and it already includes industry contacts.
- **The Copernicus SST-extremes / OMI community** — *Towards a multi-product methodology for the ocean monitoring indicator of SST extremes in the IBI region* (#23, de Pascual Collar, Alonso Valle, Gallardo, de Alfonso Alonso-Muñoyerro, Pérez Gómez, Ciliberti, Sotillo). They work on the operational Copernicus SST-extremes indicator using multi-product ensembles of regional/global models plus satellite observations — directly complementary to your heatwave early-warning forecasting, and a strong fit for the "reliable services / climate resilience" outcome.
- **The ML-for-ocean-forecasting / heatwave-prediction group** — *Ocean-E2E* (#29, Shu, Gou, Xiang, Huang) does hybrid physics-based + data-driven global MHW forecasting with end-to-end neural assimilation, the closest methodological cousin to your project. A partnership here would strengthen the "data-driven forecasting" and AI-analytics credibility of the proposal.

A note on the **industry** slot the call asks for: MonGOOS's consultation already involved 4 companies (#21), so that's the most direct route to an industry partner. I couldn't verify specific company names from what's visible to me, so I'd treat that as the one thing to confirm directly when you reach out.

If you'd like, I can pull the full text of any of these papers (#22, #21, #23, #29) to extract the exact author affiliations and contact points you'd need to start a partnership conversation.

Abstract:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

A multi-platform approach is required to address the goals outlined in the IODP science plan, including a non-riser vessel to collect widely-distributed high-resolution cores to address climate, environmental, crustal and observatory science objectives; a heavy riser-equipped vessel to reach the deep sedimentary and crustal layers; and mission-specific platforms to support high-latitude and shallow-water projects.

#22 [paper] Global Ocean Observing System status Report 2026
Authors: M. Belbéoch, Z. Begg, S. Fournier, N. Kolodziejczyk, Joanna Post, Bipendra Prakash, E. Rusciano, Laura Stukonytė
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0bd03e1cb89a8bcbb96b251c54aebf44383502c3

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for a comprehensive overview of the status, coverage, and sustainability of the global ocean observing system, including gaps in capacity and funding.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Compilation of an interactive status report aggregating statistics on national contributions, monitoring data from 17 GOOS observing networks via OceanOPS, satellite observations, and data from marine life initiatives, supplemented by qualitative impact stories.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean observations from the seafloor to the atmosphere, involving 67 countries, 17 GOOS observing networks, satellite systems, and diverse marine ecosystem initiatives.
Abstract:
The ocean underpins the safety, wellbeing and livelihoods of communities worldwide. Understanding how it is changing depends on sustained ocean observations: the measurements collected by dedicated people, instruments and platforms, from the seafloor to the atmosphere. The Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) Status Report 2026 provides an interactive overview of the status of the global ocean observing system, presents new statistics on national contributions, and showcases the societal value of ocean observations through impact stories from around the globe. Today, 67 countries contribute to physical and biogeochemical ocean observations at sea through 17 GOOS observing networks monitored by OceanOPS. Satellites complement these measurements with observations from space, while a diverse community of initiatives collects vital data on marine life and ecosystems. Together, these observations underpin weather forecasting, climate monitoring, maritime and coastal risk management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable ocean economies. The global ocean observing system continues to make progress, supported by established observing networks, long-term reference observatories, regional systems and emerging technologies. Yet, important gaps and risks remain. Observing capacity is unevenly distributed around the world, and many networks face challenges in securing the sustained funding needed to maintain and expand their observations. Strengthening coordination, improving data sharing and broadening international participation will be essential to build a more comprehensive, resilient and sustainable system. Continued investment and stronger collaboration across countries and observing communities are crucial to ensure that ocean observations can meet growing scientific, operational and societal needs. Explore the interactive GOOS Status Report to find out more.
